Imagine a shotgun with two barrels sitting side by side. That is the image at the heart of this word. A double-barreled adjective describes something that has two parts, two actions, or two effects — often happening together or aimed at the same target. The word carries a sense of doubled force, doubled purpose, or simply two-in-one.

This literal image (a gun with two barrels) extends into everyday language in several distinct ways.

In its most direct, physical sense, double-barreled simply describes a firearm with two barrels.

"He carried a double-barreled shotgun on the hunting trip."

Nothing complicated here. Two barrels. That's it. This is the root from which all figurative uses grow.
Meaning 2: Serving Two Purposes at Once / Having Two Parts

This is the most common figurative use. When something is described as double-barreled, it means it does two things simultaneously or has two components packed into one.

"She launched a double-barreled attack — criticizing both his argument and his character."

Here, the attack had two separate aims at once. Like both barrels firing together.

"His reply was a double-barreled response: an apology and a threat."

One response. Two functions. That is the spirit of this meaning.
Meaning 3: The "Double-Barreled Question" (A Very Important Special Use)

This is one of the most well-known and carefully defined uses of the word, especially in writing, journalism, debate, and research.

A double-barreled question is a question that secretly contains two separate questions but presents them as one, forcing the person to answer both at the same time — even if their answer to each would be different.

"Do you think the government should spend more on education and healthcare?"

This is double-barreled. You might think yes to education but no to healthcare. But the question forces you into a single answer for both. It is considered a flawed or unfair question because it does not let you respond honestly to each part separately.

"Was the movie entertaining and well-acted?"

Again — you might have found it entertaining but thought the acting was weak. The question does not let you say so.

This type of question is widely considered a logical fallacy and a survey design error. When someone accuses a question of being "double-barreled," they are pointing out that it is sneaking two questions into one, making it hard or impossible to give a precise, truthful answer.
Meaning 4: Very Forceful, Powerful, or Intense

Double-barreled can also simply mean having twice the force — something that hits harder, is more emphatic, or is more severe than usual.

"The company faced a double-barreled crisis: falling sales and a public scandal."

"He gave them a double-barreled warning — once in writing, once in person."

In this sense, the word suggests intensity and impact. Something double-barreled is not mild. It comes at you from two directions or with double the usual weight.
Meaning 5: A Double-Barreled Name (Especially in British English)

In Britain and many other English-speaking countries, double-barreled is used to describe a surname that combines two family names, joined by a hyphen.

"Her double-barreled surname — Hartley-Moore — came from both her parents' families."

"He introduced himself as James Worthington-Clarke."

This practice often happens when two families marry and want both names to continue, or for social, legal, or personal reasons. The hyphen between the two names is the visual "double barrel." This use is especially common and recognizable in British English, where such names have a long cultural history and are sometimes associated with upper-class or aristocratic families — though they are used by people of all backgrounds today.

Here is a quick mental map of all the ways you will encounter this word:

  • A double-barreled gun → literally has two barrels.
  • A double-barreled question → unfairly combines two separate questions into one; considered a logical flaw.
  • A double-barreled attack / effort / strategy → hits from two sides or serves two purposes at once.
  • A double-barreled name → a hyphenated surname combining two family names (e.g., Smith-Jones).

No matter which sense you encounter, the word always carries the same underlying idea: two things joined together, acting as one. Sometimes that doubling is practical (two names, two purposes). Sometimes it is powerful (double the force). Sometimes it is a problem (a question that should have been two separate questions). But the essential image — two barrels, side by side — never really disappears.
